residual_risks.why_it_matters: Resolving a datasource key to its ORM class is done by scanning `Base.registry.mappers` for a matching `local_table.name`, and that loop is written three times: query_engine._model_for (line 71), datasource_registry._add_primary_keys (line 577), and datasource_registry.primary_key_field (line 553). Two of the three live in the same file, 25 lines apart. The registry's two import-time mutation hooks (`_add_primary_keys()` at line 607, `_add_project_columns()` at line 634) exist so a new auto-registered column needs no per-source edit — but each hook re-implements the scan, so registering a third auto-column means writing a fourth loop rather than one more line.

residual_risks.note: `builder_service._attr` is a thin wrapper reaching into `query_engine` internals.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: `_attr(source, field_name)` is `getattr(qe._model_for(ds), field_name)` — a pass-through that adds no behavior, needs a `# noqa: SLF001` because it calls another module's private helper, and skips the registry field validation that `query_engine._column` performs. It is called twice, for `join_field` and for the hardcoded `project_id`. The module already routes everything else through the public `qe.*` surface (build_select/apply_filters/apply_sort/paginate); this is the one path where a field name reaches `getattr` unchecked, so a typo in a join rule surfaces as an AttributeError instead of the registry's 400.

residual_risks.note: `_ctx_session` duplicates `worker.session_scope` and never closes the session it opens. Folded into the P0 at #2, which fixes the same function.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: worker.py already owns 'ARQ ctx → AsyncSession' twice over (`session_scope`, which closes, and `_make_session`, which does not); report_tasks adds a third accessor that reads `ctx.get('session_factory')` itself and raises its own RuntimeError. Worse, `reclaim_stale_report_tasks` uses it and never closes the session — the exact leak `session_scope` was introduced to make structurally impossible (worker.py:74-84 records that both task bodies previously forgot). The cron therefore leaks one connection per fire, and the fix is a one-line deletion rather than an addition.

residual_risks.note: The verify rate limit is an in-process counter. This is only a risk if the app is deployed with more than one process, and no repository evidence establishes the deployment topology (no uvicorn `--workers` setting found), so it is recorded rather than asserted.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: `/verify/{id}` is the one unauthenticated route in the P8 surface (免登录), and its only brute-force/abuse protection is `check_rate_limit`, an in-process dict guarded by a module-level asyncio.Lock. With N uvicorn workers the effective limit is N × `report_verify_rate_limit`, and the states are not shared — so the protection is weakest exactly in the horizontally-scaled deployment it is most needed in. Separately, `_WINDOW_STATE.setdefault(key, deque())` never removes keys: eviction happens only inside a request for that same key, and the only other entry point is `clear_all_rate_limits()` (test/ops only). An unauthenticated attacker rotating source IPs grows the dict without bound for the process lifetime. The pre-existing implementation is documented as single-instance-only; the finding is that this new public endpoint inherits that limitation without a compensating control (no signature check happens before the limiter, so unauthenticated callers can consume the window).

residual_risks.note: The HMAC signature does not bind to the client IP. That is a deliberate consequence of the feature: the URL is printed on a QR code and scanned by field staff on a different network.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: `_check_sig` binds the signature to `(report_file_id, exp)` only. The IP rate-limit (`check_rate_limit`) is a best-effort throttle, not part of the signature. A signature extracted from one PDF is reusable from any IP for the full 15-minute TTL — the only gate is the per-IP throttle of 30/min, which is trivial to evade by spreading requests across many addresses (botnet, IPv6 /64 prefix rotation, VPN). The QR is printed on the PDF, so the signature is not a secret — but binding the client IP into the HMAC would force an attacker who stole a QR URL to also replay from the original scanning device, which raises the cost of QR phishing.

residual_risks.note: The IP rate limit trusts `client.host`, which behind a reverse proxy is the proxy's address. Depends on the same unestablished deployment topology as the item above.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: `_client_ip` returns `request.client.host` directly. Behind a reverse proxy (the standard production deployment for FastAPI/uvicorn), `request.client` is the proxy's IP, not the caller's. The rate-limit key `report_verify:{ip}` collapses every site scan behind the same proxy into one bucket. Two consequences: (1) a single user can exceed the limit and cause legitimate scans of other users to 429, and (2) an attacker can flood from many IPs all sharing the same upstream, but those all funnel to the same bucket and a modest botnet still defeats the throttle. The diff's helper documents the httpx-vs-uvicorn shape mismatch but does not consider trusted-proxy header parsing.

residual_risks.note: Style patches are stored verbatim, so users can write arbitrary JSON keys into `style_json`. The renderer tolerates unknown keys, so this is a tidiness concern rather than a defect.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: `create`/`revise` accept the user-supplied `patch: dict` and write it directly into `ReportStyleRow.style_json` (JSONB). The Pydantic schema (`StylePatch`) forbids two keys (`font_dir`, `locked_fields`) at the API boundary, but only those two. Any other unrecognized key would be rejected by `StylePatch.model_config = {'extra': 'forbid'}` — verified. **However**, the patch dictionary is then validated back into `ReportStyle(**row.style_json)` at read time (`_summary`), and Pydantic will silently drop extra keys on `ReportStyle.model_validate` unless `extra='allow'` is set (it isn't, but `.model_validate` on an unrelated `style_json` could still raise). The realistic risk is that future schema additions end up accepting more fields than intended, since the `STYLE_FIELDS_NOT_WRITABLE` allowlist lives in one place (the schema) and any reader that bypasses it (e.g., a future ad-hoc endpoint or background job reading `style_json` directly) sees the raw JSON.

residual_risks.note: `definition_json.OutputFormat` is overwritten by the `output_format` column on every write. The docstring documents the column as authoritative, so this is a documented contract -- but it is surprising enough to note.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: `ReportDefinitionBody` publishes `OutputFormat` (and `MaxRows`) as part of the documented definition body, and the frontend sends them there (definitionBody.ts:204-205). On every create/update the service overwrites those two keys with the top-level columns unconditionally, so a client that sets `definition_json.OutputFormat = "xlsx"` while leaving the top-level `output_format` at its `"pdf"` default gets HTTP 201 with the requested value silently discarded -- the response comes back showing `"pdf"`. This is precisely the failure class schemas/report_builder.py:133-137 says `extra="forbid"` was added to prevent ('save succeeded but nothing changed'), except here the field is accepted, echoed, and then overwritten. Clients cannot tell which of the two locations is authoritative from the contract; SPEC §3.2.2(2) lists them as siblings in the definition body.

`update()` accepts `project_id` as a parameter and writes `row.project_id = project_id`. There's no check that the actor has access to the new project (only `_reject_duplicate` which is name-uniqueness within a project). A creator with access to project A and project B could move a definition from A to B by editing it. The endpoint `update_definition` in `report_builder.py` passes `body.project_id` straight through. Combined with the status rollback to DRAFT on edit, this can quietly relocate definitions across projects — and once re-published, anyone with access to B sees it.

residual_risks.note: The demo limit counts OBSOLETE definitions toward the cap.
residual_risks.why_it_matters: `_check_demo_limit` runs `select(ReportDefinition.def_id)` with no `WHERE` clause, so it counts DRAFT + PUBLISHED + OBSOLETE rows. After the user obsoletes some, the counter doesn't drop and they hit the 403 even though fewer visible defs exist. The docstring acknowledges this is intentional ("全库" not "按用户") but doesn't justify counting OBSOLETE, which by design is excluded from the default list. For demo deployments this caps the user at 3 lifetime definitions unless they get someone to manually delete rows.

testing_gaps.note: CORRECTED CLAIM. The reviewer's P1 -- 'all 15 filter operators are never executed' -- is false: all 15 appear in tests/ (per-operator grep counts: IN 26, GT 14, EQ 12, LT 6, IS_NULL 5, BETWEEN 3, IS_NOT_NULL 3, NEQ 2, NOT_IN 2, CONTAINS 2, LIKE 2, STARTS_WITH 1, ENDS_WITH 1, GTE 1, LTE 1). What survives is narrower: no test ever calls `apply_filters` against a JSONB-backed column, so the `->>` branch of the filter compiler has no end-to-end coverage. The reviewer's companion claim that this is a production 500 on Postgres is unproven -- `->>` is valid PG syntax, and tests/conftest.py:51,101 installs SQLite JSONB shims -- so it is not asserted here.
testing_gaps.why_it_matters: One SQL dialect branch in the filter compiler is unexercised; nothing else in the operator surface is untested.

testing_gaps.note: All 4 cases call `builder_service.execute_definition`; the fixed-10-types `collect` path has no project-scope test at all, which is why the P0 at #1 was never caught.
The last-attempt retry assertion cannot distinguish an ARQ `Retry` from the original error being re-raised.
testing_gaps.why_it_matters: Both task bodies end their failure handler with a contract the tests explicitly document: on the final attempt the task must re-raise the *original* exception so ARQ can mark the job dead, and only on earlier attempts may it raise `Retry`. The test asserting this uses `pytest.raises(RuntimeError)` — but `arq.Retry` is declared `class Retry(RuntimeError)` at arq/worker.py:97, so `pytest.raises(RuntimeError)` catches `Retry` too. The assertion therefore stays green if someone deletes the `if attempt_no < MAX_TRIES:` guard and raises `Retry` unconditionally, which is precisely the bug the docstring says it exists to prevent: ARQ re-enqueues forever, 'retries are exhausted' never reaches the job result, and the row is never given a terminal state. The first `pytest.raises(Retry)` assertion in the same test is fine; it is only the symmetric 'last attempt' half that is vacuous. Tighten both to distinguish the exception types.

testing_gaps.note: Pixel-level visual renderer tests never run in any gate.
testing_gaps.why_it_matters: `tests/services/report/test_renderer_visual.py` exists for one stated reason: the footer-page-number class of bug where the PDF text layer contains the right characters but nothing is actually painted on the page, so every `extract_text()` assertion goes green. `pyproject.toml` sets `addopts = "-m 'not visual'"`, so those four tests are deselected in every default `pytest` invocation. The marker documentation and the module docstring both defer to CI (`CI 用 pytest -m visual 跑`), but the repository's only workflow, `.github/workflows/check-api-drift.yml`, runs alembic + OpenAPI drift + a migration idempotency guard and never invokes pytest — so the compensating control does not exist either. I ran them manually (`pytest -m visual`): 4 passed, so the tests are not broken — they are simply inert, and the renderer regression class they were built for has no automated gate. Either wire them into a gate that actually runs, or accept in writing that renderer layout regressions are caught only by a human remembering to type the flag.

testing_gaps.note: The SPEC source contract for 9 of 10 report types is unpacked and discarded.
testing_gaps.why_it_matters: The module docstring states the rule it is enforcing — '每种的源与格式都来自 SPEC … 「泵数据表」必须出在 `PUMP_RESULTS`'. The test unpacks both halves of the hard-coded SPEC table but binds the source half to `_expected_source` and never asserts on it. Consequently only the format half is enforced for all ten types; the source half is enforced for exactly one (`test_energy_calc_book_source_matches_spec`). If `PUMP_DATA_TABLE.primary` were changed to `UTIL_RESULTS`, `test_each_type_declares_a_real_datasource` and `test_primary_source_is_among_sources` would both still pass, because they only check internal consistency, never the SPEC mapping — and a user would silently get utility data in a pump data table. Assert the source as well.

triage_groups.title: Report query assembly breaks the row-limit contract and races on dedup
triage_groups.context: All three sit in the collect/store path: a hard batch ceiling that contradicts the advertised 100,000 rows (#5), a chunked IN loop that ANDs chunks into an empty intersection (#20), and a content-addressed finalize that collides and then rolls back the caller's whole transaction (#22).
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: #5 first -- it is a user-visible contract break with a one-line fix. #20 next. #22 needs the recovery path reworked.

triage_groups.title: Execution page poll and fetch lifecycle
triage_groups.context: One page, one shared timer ref, no cancellation token. #7 (no cancellation) and #8 (FAILED never read) are the two P1s; #10 and #11 are the fetch-side consequences.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: #7 then #8 -- both are localized to `poll()`. #11 needs a product decision (what 'cleared temporary filters' should mean) before the code changes.
triage_groups.why: Same function, same file, one guard fixes the top two.

triage_groups.title: Definition semantics dropped between save and execution
triage_groups.context: SortBy direction is stored in the definition and never read (#9); the two output-format whitelists disagree so csv works on one endpoint and not the other (#19).
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Pass `direction` through to the sort clause; make both endpoints read one whitelist constant.
triage_groups.why: Both are 'saved successfully, ignored at run time' -- the exact failure the format-whitelist docstring already warns about.

triage_groups.title: Migration and database invariants
triage_groups.context: `p8_001` creates a unique constraint that Postgres will not enforce for NULL `project_id` (#14) and a downgrade that drops the audit tables outright (#15).
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: #14: `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+) or a partial unique index, in a new revision. #15: decide the downgrade policy (refuse, or archive first) -- that is a product decision.
triage_groups.why: Both are irreversible once someone runs them; #15 changes what an operator is allowed to do.

triage_groups.title: Frontend style and filter editor gaps
triage_groups.context: #12 says an existing style can never be revised from the UI although the backend endpoint exists; #25 and #30 silently mutate or drop filter nodes; #26 keys rows by index next to move buttons.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: #26 is mechanical (stable key). #25 and #30 need a decision: reject loudly or repair silently. #12 needs a design call on whether revising belongs on this page.
triage_groups.why: Three of the four are one-file edits; the open question is intended behaviour, not code.

triage_groups.context: Mechanical, low-risk, and unrelated to each other: the `pcs_test` database is behind, no `docs/solutions/` writeback for 12 P8 fixes, two error envelopes in the same router, an application-only ACTIVE-style invariant, stale MSW mocks, an ignored status filter, and two small contract/type nits.
